Have there been any games that work better with virtual reality than without?
Anything where you need to estimate distances somewhat accurately?
I don't have a vr system, but I think Elite:Dangerous would probably work really well, same with any flight sim

It does, and it doesn't. For dogfighting, yes - it can work exceptionally well provided you have the right HOTAS setup.

OTOH, it's really bad for anything where you have to look things up. For example, if you're running cargo and need to make notes about cargo availability and routes VR makes that difficult. VR only works when everything you need to play the game is in the game.

I have an Oculus Rift. I really love it and have no regrets, but I don't know that I'd recommend that someone else buy one just yet.

As for your question, sure. A lot of stuff is being done badly, but some games work exceptionally well in VR and are definitely improved by it.

Vehicle simulations in particular are really great in VR. Things like Elite Dangerous, Sublevel Zero, Descent Underground, Project Cars, EVE: Valkyre, Assetto Corsa, Euro Truck Simulator, and a handful of other titles are amazing in VR.

Other stuff works too if done right. Lucky's Tale is a really great little platformer for example. It does interesting things with VR and using it made it better than the completely generic game it would have been otherwise.

First person stuff can be more immersive using it, which can be an improvement depending on the game. There aren't a ton of games that do this well right now. There are injector programs that allow you to play stuff like Skyrim, Borderlands, Grand Theft Auto V in 1st person mode, and a lot of other games as well.

However, using an injector program generally only really offers a glimpse of potential, and small issues add up making playing those games that way little more than a novelty at the moment. You can see where it might be great in the future, but currently it's not really an improvement to play them that way outside of the novelty of using VR for them.

The Zombie game Dying light is also improved by using VR. Horror in general really is improved by it. However, there's not a lot out there that uses it. Alien Isolation was really great, but no longer supports VR. However, they have announced that they're bringing back support in the future. A monster is a lot scarier than it is on a monitor when it actually looks eight feet tall and like it's about to rip your face off.

Subnautica and World of Diving are also really great VR showcases.

Generally speaking, stuff that forces you to stand up and use motion controls, limits the area to 'room space', or has you on rails, is basically just a glorified tech demo.

Some games that were surprisingly improved by VR quite a bit are the original Doom, Doom II, and Duke Nukem 3D. They're great fun using a VR headset. Grid based movement RPGs also work exceptionally well, such as Legend of Grimrock and Might and Magic III.

Minecraft is also improved by it. Though, not in the way you might expect. Playing the game itself is neat and a fun novelty, but the best part of it is visiting some of the servers where huge build projects have been going on. For example, I visited the Disney World and Middle Earth servers and it was amazing to walk around looking at all the cool stuff in VR. There are some seriously impressive things to see on many Minecraft servers, not all of which are related to fiction, but some impressive original stuff, and even real world places recreated such as the entire country of Denmark.

In my experience, the best stuff is games you can play seated with a controller, or sim type games that have you in the cockpit or driver's seat of something interesting.

The stand up and motion control stuff tends to be gimmicky and limited a lot more. Stuff built around the hardware rather than games that integrate it. As a result, they tend to be small, simplistic, and boring.

Though there aren't any real examples of it yet, I can also see management games, God Games, top down 3/4 view RPGs, strategy, and RTS games such as Starcraft, The Sims, Divinity Original Sin, Diablo, Cities, X-com, and Civilization working really well in VR. Having the board set up on a virtual 'table' in front of you that you can move around in, lean in, and turn would be a really interesting way to play something like that. Thing is, it would have to be designed for VR to work.

Also, rollercoaster simulators are a ton of fun. I have No Limits 2 and it's amazing in VR. Though, not for those who get motion sick. If you're into coasters, it's a complete blast though.

There are a few shining examples that offer a glimpse into what VR can be. However, right now there isn't much out there and a lot of developers seem lost and confused about what exactly to do with VR. VR needs more time to develop before it's really ready as a consumer product to be honest. If you're thinking of buying one, I'd hold out for a bit to see how things develop. What's out there is a lot of fun, but flawed. There are really only a handful of titles that are really improved by VR, and a metric ton of gimmicky glorified tech demos.

We need a little time for developers to figure out what to do with VR, and then a bit more for some decent games with a full development cycle behind them to get released.

The only caveat to that is if you're into vehicle sim games, such as driving games, flight sims, or space sims. It's totally worth a purchase if that's your thing. Far better than a multi-monitor setup. Particularly if you have a Wheel and HOTAS setup. Otherwise, wait for the technology to develop a bit before diving in.

This is unfortunately an area where I see "the cloud" as a necessity. There's no real way for a small operation be it a home user or small business to take on that many requests/traffic. It's basically going to have to work like insurance where people pay in to a service that can handle such situations if they arise for you.
